Planning by Dynamic Programming

“Dynamic”

Sequential/temporal component

“Programming”

Optimising a “program” / policy

Properties of DP

Dynamic programming is a general solution method for problems with 2 properties:

Property Presence in RL
Optimal substructure (optimal solution can be decomposed into subproblems) Bellman equation gives recursive decomposition
Overlapping subproblems which recur many times - solutions can be cached and reused Value function is the subproblem that can be cached

DP Assumptions

Assumes full knowledge of the MDP Used for planning in an MDP

Prediction Control
Input:
1. $\text{MDP}\braket{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R},\gamma}$ or MRP $\text{MDP}\braket{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P}^\pi,\mathcal{R}^\pi,\gamma}$
2. Policy $\pi$		 Input:
1. $\text{MDP}\braket{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R},\gamma}$
Output:
1. Value function $v_\pi$
 Output:
1. Optimal value function $v_$
2. Optimal policy $\pi_$

Policy Evaluation

Problem

Evaluate a given policy $\pi$

Solution

Iterative application of Bellman expectation backup

$v_1\to v_2\to…\to v_\pi$ Using synchronous backups At each iteration $k+1$ For all states $s\in S$ Update $v_{k+1}(s)$ from $v_k(s’)$ where $s’$ is a successor state of $s$

$v_{k+1}=\sum_{a\in A}\pi(a\vert s)(\mathcal{R}^a_s+\gamma\sum_{s’ \in S}\mathcal{P}^a_{ss’}v_k(s’))$ $v^{k+1}=\mathcal{R}^\pi+\gamma\mathcal{P}^\pi v^k$

Policy Iteration

  1. Evaluate the policy $\pi$ in $v_\pi=\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{R}{t+1}+\gamma\mathcal{R}{t+2}+…\vert S_t=s]$
  2. Improve the policy by acting greedily with respect to $v_\pi$ -> $\pi’=\text{greedy}(v_\pi)$

Policy iteration always converges to $\pi^*$

Policy evaluation (Estimate $v_\pi$) $\rightleftarrows$ Policy improvement (Generate $\pi’\ge\pi$)

Policy Improvement Theorem

Imagine we start with a deterministic policy $a=\pi(s)$

We can improve the policy by acting greedily $\pi ‘(s)=\arg\max_{a\in A}q_\pi(s,a)$ This improves the value from any state $s$ over one step: $q_\pi(s,\pi’(s))=\max_{a\in A}q_\pi(s,a)\ge q_\pi(s,\pi(s))=v_\pi(s)$

$q_\pi$(s,a) - Value gained if we use policy $\pi$ from state $s$ and taking action $a$

$q_\pi(s,\pi’(s))=\mathbb{E}{\pi’}[R{t+1}+\gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1})\vert S_t=s]$ $\le \mathbb{E}{\pi’}[R{t+1}+\gamma R_{t+2}+…\vert S_t=s]=v_{\pi’}(S)$

If improvements stop $q_\pi(s,\pi’(s))=\max_{a\in A}q_\pi(s,a)=q_\pi(s,\pi(s))=v_\pi(s)$ Then the Bellman optimality equation has been satisfied $v_\pi(s)=\max_{a\in A}q_\pi(s,a)$ $v_\pi(s)=v_*(s)$ $\forall s\in S$

If policy improvement stops -> Bellman optimality equation satisfied -> Found an optimal policy

Policy iteration solves MDPs $v_\pi(s)=\max_{a\in A}q_\pi(s,a)$ $v_\pi(s)=v_*(s)$ for all $s\in S$

Modified Policy Iteration

Early stopping $\epsilon$-convergence of value function (when value function only changing by $\epsilon$) Or stop evaluating policy after $k$ iterations

Value iteration

Principle of Optimality Theorem

Policy $\pi(a\vert s)$ achieves optimal value $v_\pi(s)=v_(s)$ from state $s$ iff: For any state $s’$ reachable from $s$, $\pi$ achieves the optimal value from state $s’$, $v_\pi(s’)=v_(s’)$

Value Iteration Algorithm

If we know the solution to subproblems $v_*(s’)$

Then solution $v_(s)$ can be found by one-step lookahead $v_(s)\leftarrow\max_{a\in A}R^a_s+\gamma\sum_{s’in S}P^a_{ss’}v_*(s’)$

Value iteration applies these updates again and again

Intuition

Start at the end of the problem and work back Still works with loopy, stochastic MDPs

Problem

Find optimal policy $\pi$

Solution

Iterative application of Bellman optimality backup $v_1\to v_2\to …\to v_*$ Using synchronous backups

  • At each iteration $k+1$
  • For all states $s\in S$
  • Update $v_{k+1}(s)$ from $v_k(s’)$

Unlike policy iteration, there is no explicit policy Intermediate value functions may not achievable by any policy

This is modified policy iteration with $k=1$ ![[Pasted image 20261101211533.png]] The curve below the first open circle means $\max$

Each state performs a lookahead and finds a new value $v_{k+1}(s)\leftarrow s$

$v_{k+1}(s)=\max_{a\in A}(R^a_s+\gamma\sum_{s’\in S}P^a_{ss’}v_k(s’))$ $v_{k+1}=\max_{a\in A}(R^a+\gamma P^av_k)$

Problem Bellman Equation Algorithm
Prediction Bellman Expectation Equation Iterative Policy Evaluation
Control Bellman Expectation Equation + Greedy Policy Improvement Policy Iteration
Control Bellman Optimality Equation Value Iteration

Algorithms are based on state-value function $v_\pi(s)$ or $v_*(s)$ Complexity $O(mn^2)$ per iteration for $m$ actions and $n$ states

Could apply $q$ updates -> $O(m^2n^2)$

Dynamic Programming Extensions

Asynchronous DP

$v_{\text{new}(s)}\leftarrow\max_{a\in A}(R^a_s+\gamma\sum_{s’\in S}P^a_{ss’}v_{\text{old}}(s’))$ $v_{\text{old}}\leftarrow v_{\text{new}}$ Instead do $v(s)\leftarrow\max_{a\in A}(R^a_s+\gamma\sum_{s’\in S}P^a_{ss’}v(s’))$

Prioritised Sweeping

Use magnitude of Bellman error to guide state selection. $\vert \max_{a\in A}(R^a_s+\gamma\sum_{s’\in S}P^a_{ss’}v(s’))-v(s)\vert $

  • Backup the state with the largest Bellman error
  • Update Bellman error of affected states after each backup
  • Requires knowledge of reverse dynamics (predecessor states)
  • Can be implemented efficiently by maintaining a priority queue

    Real-time Dynamic Programming

  • Idea: only states that are relevant to agent
  • Use agent’s experience to guide the selection of states
  • After each time-step $S_t,A_t,R_{t+1}$
  • Backup the state $S_t$ $v(S_t)\leftarrow\max_{a\in A}(R^a_{S_t}+\gamma\sum_{s’\in S}P^a_{S_ts’}v(s’))$

    DP Curse of Dimensionality

    For each backup, every successor state and actions is stored Number of states $n=\vert S\vert $ grows exponentially with number of variables Can be too expensive for even one backup with $10^{170}$ states

    SOLUTION -> Sample

    1. Sample one action according to policy
    2. Sample transition according to dynamics
    3. Backup based off 1 sample, rather than branching factor

Advantages:

  1. Model-free - no advance knowledge required: Rather than someone having to tell us dynamics, we sample to find out
  2. Breaks curse of dimensionality
  3. Costs of backups is consistent
